title: Beyond words
hook: Moses runs after the shepherd, who has gone past speech altogether (Masnavi 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses is rebuked: God told him he was sent to unite, not to sever. Your line was their words, not mine. Whose words did you hear differently? Day one hundred ninety-six.

Running after someone to apologize goes like this. Out the door, down the street, heart going, rehearsing the words. And sometimes, on catching up, it turns out they've already moved on. Not in anger. They've just gone somewhere that can't quite be followed anymore. That's where our story ends. Moses has been rebuked. He knows he has to find the shepherd and set things right. So the prophet goes out into the desert, running. Today, the last part of the story: beyond words.
screen: `RUNNING AFTER SOMEONE TO APOLOGIZE.` → `INTO THE DESERT.` → `BEYOND WORDS.`

segments.voice: Rumi gives us a lovely detail. Moses follows the shepherd's footprints in the sand, and they're all over the place. The steps of someone lost in his own heart: one like a castle on a chessboard, going straight, another like a bishop, going slantwise. Finally Moses catches up. And he brings good news. You have permission, he says. Don't look for rules or proper forms. Say whatever your heart wants to say. Your way of praying is the light of faith. It sounds like the happy ending. It isn't. The shepherd answers: Moses, I've gone past that now. I'm soaked in my heart's blood. In Rumi's telling he says he has passed beyond the Lote Tree, the tree that in Islamic tradition marks the farthest boundary of heaven. You struck my horse with your whip, he tells Moses, and it leapt and went beyond the sky. And then he says this. My state now is beyond telling. What I'm saying to you isn't my state. The scolding didn't just hurt him. It pushed him past the need for words altogether. Rumi then turns to the reader. Whatever you say in praise of God, he says, is like the image a mirror shows. The picture is yours, not the mirror's. On Rumi's reading, our words about the sacred are never the sacred itself. Even the proper ones. Even Moses's. Yesterday was about not judging someone's words. Today goes one step further: at the deepest point, maybe no words fit. Your line: beyond words.
screen: `FOOTPRINTS LIKE CHESS PIECES.` · `YOU HAVE PERMISSION.` · `I'VE GONE PAST THAT NOW.` · then, large: `BEYOND WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit wordless for a minute, or two. Settle. Let the words in your head slow down, the way traffic thins late at night. When a sentence starts, you don't have to finish it. Just let it trail off. Rest in whatever is there before the words. If you pray, this can be a prayer with nothing said. The bell holds the time.
Beyond words. Moses runs after the shepherd to give him permission to pray his own way, and finds he has gone past speech altogether. Today's word.
Your line: beyond words. Today, once, when you feel something big, a view, a laugh, a loss, don't describe it. Just let it be bigger than your words. Day one hundred ninety-six.

screen: `DAY 196 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE OBSTACLE BECOMES THE WAY.`

howItsDone: Many traditions keep a practice of silent prayer or contemplation alongside spoken prayer, and some of Rumi's lyric poems close on the word for silent.

fork.setup: you're the shepherd. Moses has run across the desert to tell you that you can pray any way you like. what do you say?
options: thank you; I'll go back to combing God's hair.
I'm still angry; leave me alone.
I've gone past that now; my state is beyond telling.
fork.reveal: the shepherd says the scolding sent him beyond the sky, and that what he says is no longer his state.

original.note: Persian: silent, hushed. some of Rumi's lyric poems close on this word.

trapdoor: what you thought: the shepherd gets his old prayer back.
what it means: he has gone past needing words at all.
what a scholar hears: the Lote Tree, sidrat al-muntaha, the boundary of heaven in the Qur'an and the Prophet's night journey, and the ghazals of Rumi that close on khamush, 'be silent'.

sources.work: The Qur'an (the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary, described)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook reworded (no 'you've maybe'); 'Imagine the shepherd hearing that' and 'the most important thing' removed; bishop now moves slantwise, not sideways; the claim that our words are never the sacred is attributed to Rumi's reading; 'so often' / 'best-known voices' / 'many' ghazals softened to 'some'.

Paraphrased from Nicholson: the scattered footprints (chess-piece image), Moses's message of permission ('seek no rules'), the shepherd's reply (soaked in heart's blood, beyond the Lote Tree, whip and horse leaping beyond the heavens, 'my state is beyond telling'), and Rumi's mirror image. Confirm each detail, especially which chess pieces Rumi names.
The Lote Tree (sidrat al-muntaha) at Qur'an 53:14: confirm reference and 'farthest boundary of heaven' phrasing.
Khamush as a closing word in many of Rumi's ghazals: confirm.
